plot_extraction.response_text:
Newly dressed in long trousers, Abner decides to make his first formal social call on Champe Claiborne, guided by a book of etiquette. He recruits his friend Ross, and the nervous boys rehearse proper conversation, dress carefully, and prepare calling cards. Once at the Claiborne home, however, they are too intimidated and confused to announce their purpose. The family assumes they have simply come to visit, feeds them supper, includes them in the evening’s activities, and even puts them to bed for the night.

The next morning, the household openly delights in the boys’ embarrassment. Before they can finally declare that they came to call on Champe, a messenger arrives with a humiliating threat from Abner’s mother, sending Abner fleeing home. Ross starts after him, but Champe’s mocking laughter makes him turn back. In a burst of courage, he kisses her in front of the entire household and then leaves triumphantly, dodging the stones she playfully throws after him.

style_extraction.response_text:
The story is a comic coming-of-age farce rendered in a richly observant, gently satirical style. Its humour arises from the collision between adolescent self-importance and ordinary social reality: the boys attempt to imitate adult courtship through rigid etiquette, but their rehearsed formulas prove useless in a household that treats them as children. The narrative sustains affectionate mockery rather than cruelty. Abner’s pretension, Ross’s anxiety, and the adults’ amused awareness are exaggerated for comic effect, yet the boys’ humiliation remains emotionally credible.

The narration uses a flexible third-person omniscient perspective, moving freely between external description, authorial commentary, and the private fears of the two protagonists. It often inhabits the boys’ inflated understanding of events while retaining an adult ironic distance. Minor obstacles therefore acquire mock-heroic dimensions: a clean collar becomes oppressive, Aunt Missouri is as terrifying as “a lion in the way,” and an awkward visit assumes the gravity of a military expedition or religious ordeal. Occasional direct interventions—such as “Oh, youth—youth—youth, with its rash promises!”—strengthen the voice of a knowing storyteller looking back indulgently on adolescent folly.

The prose mixes elevated, literary diction with colloquial rural speech. Narrative phrases such as “pregnant silence,” “inferential invitation,” “psychological moment,” and “served his novitiate” lend ceremonious weight to trivial incidents. This is deliberately contrasted with compressed dialogue such as “I ain’t goin’,” “Fire away,” and “let’s cut and run.” The disparity between registers is one of the story’s main comic engines. Abner’s etiquette manual introduces a third idiom: stiff, prescriptive, and socially aspirational. Its formulas—“Let a rich stream of conversation flow,” “Name yours,” and “You flatter us”—sound absurd when repeated mechanically by frightened country boys.

Sentence structure is varied and generally expansive. Long, carefully balanced sentences accumulate qualifications, emotional reactions, and comic detail, while short sentences or fragments punctuate moments of alarm: “Oh, Lord!”; “Breakfast!”; “They’ve put us to bed!” Parallel constructions and repetition heighten the farce, particularly in sequences describing what the boys fail to do: “They did not rise. They did not thunder out anything.” Lists and escalating clauses allow embarrassment to build incrementally, turning each attempted solution into a new complication.

The dialogue is highly characterising. Abner speaks with borrowed loftiness whenever he feels secure, but lapses into panic and aggression when his performance is threatened. Ross is more sceptical, concrete, and honest; his literal questions expose the impracticality of the etiquette book. Aunt Missouri’s speech is warm, practical, and teasing, while the servants’ dialogue is represented through strongly marked historical Southern eye dialect. Contractions, altered spellings, nonstandard grammar, and phonetic approximations establish regional and social distinctions. This dialect treatment is integral to the period setting, though it also reflects dated racial conventions and stereotypes.

Description is selective, vivid, and frequently figurative. Physical details serve both characterisation and comedy: Ross’s freckles “advertised a rich soil,” the boys lean together like “young saplings weakened at the root,” and Babe trembles “like chocolate pudding.” Clothing and bodily gestures recur as motifs of insecurity. Collars wilt, hats are crushed or clutched, knees collapse, tongues stiffen, and faces redden or whiten. These visible signs translate inner panic into theatrical action. The repeated attention to hats, cards, collars, ties, and polished shoes also underscores the story’s concern with outward performance and social status.

The setting is a small Southern community governed by Sunday customs, family familiarity, and close communal observation. The white road, porch, arbor, dining room, servants, and plantation-style household create a specific regional world. Social privacy is almost nonexistent: mothers notice clean shirts, neighbors know one another’s children, household servants participate in the joke, and the boys fear that their failure will become village-wide knowledge. The setting therefore intensifies their predicament by making embarrassment public and inescapable.

Structurally, the story follows a sustained escalation. It begins with Abner preparing his appearance, adds Ross as an unwilling accomplice, introduces the etiquette manual as a flawed plan, and then delays the intended call through a chain of misunderstandings. The boys fail to announce themselves, are invited to supper, endure evening entertainment, are mistakenly kept overnight, and face a laughing audience at breakfast. Repeated opportunities to explain themselves create comic suspense because each chance is missed. The climax arrives when Abner’s mother publicly summons him home and he flees, after which Ross converts humiliation into decisive action by kissing Champe before everyone. The ending releases the accumulated tension and completes Ross’s development from paralysed imitator to spontaneous actor.

The dominant narrative techniques are irony, incongruity, repetition, escalation, and delayed resolution. Situational irony governs the whole plot: the boys go to demonstrate maturity but are fed, supervised, and put to bed as children. Verbal irony appears in the narrator’s grandiose labels for their enterprise and in the gap between the etiquette book’s promises and its practical effects. Running jokes—the undelivered card, the perpetually clutched hats, the inability to state the purpose of the visit—give the episode cohesion.

Thematically, the story explores the awkward transition from childhood to adulthood, the artificiality of learned social codes, and the difference between performance and genuine confidence. Abner depends on scripts, clothing, and status symbols, so interruption destroys his composure. Ross initially submits to the same “hypnotism,” but ultimately acts without a script. His impulsive kiss is socially outrageous, yet within the comic logic of the story it constitutes authentic courage. The final tone is triumphant and affectionate: embarrassment becomes initiation, and failed imitation gives way to self-possession.

generation.response_text:
## Abner’s First Call

The first pair of long trousers came to Abner Talcott on a Saturday afternoon, and by Sunday morning they had altered not merely the visible length of his legs, but his understanding of society, his obligations toward the female sex, and, in some degree, the destiny of the human race.

They were gray trousers, cut with an amplitude which suggested that the tailor had faith in Abner’s future. At present they hung somewhat mournfully from his hips and broke over his shoes in folds; but Abner saw in the mirror no such defects. He saw a young gentleman standing upon the solemn threshold of manhood. Behind him lay marbles, bare knees, fishing worms, pantry raids, and the undignified habit of sliding down banisters. Before him opened a shining avenue of calls, compliments, business engagements, perhaps duels.

His mother, who had brought the trousers home wrapped in brown paper, viewed their spiritual effect with less enthusiasm.

“You needn’t stand there looking like the governor,” she said. “Go fetch me some kindling.”

Abner turned slowly from the glass.

“In these?”

“In those or without them.”

A cruel world has ever begun by assigning kindling to its statesmen.

He obeyed, but he carried the basket with a remote air, as if he had consented to the task only because great men must sometimes humor domestic institutions. Upon returning, he brushed two chips from his knee, resumed his station before the parlor mirror, and began considering whom he ought first to honor with a formal call.

The name of Champe Claiborne occurred to him almost immediately.

Champe was thirteen, red-haired, freckled across the nose, and given to speaking the truth at moments when truth was least becoming. She could climb the mulberry tree better than Abner, had once beaten him in a foot race, and had thrown a green apple at him during Sunday-school picnic exercises. None of these circumstances disqualified her. On the contrary, they invested the project with danger; and danger, contemplated in long trousers before a mirror, is exceedingly attractive.

Moreover, Champe’s father owned the big white house beyond the locust grove, with six porch columns, a dinner bell, an arbor, and a gravel carriage sweep. The Claibornes received callers. Abner had seen buggies draw up there on Sunday evenings, and young men with canes disappear through the front door. It followed that Champe, though regrettably familiar with his childhood crimes, was a lady upon whom one might call.

The difficulty was that Abner did not know how.

Providence—or some agency less benevolent—had prepared for this. In the glass-fronted bookcase stood a volume entitled *The Young Gentleman’s Social Guide and Manual of Polite Deportment*. It had belonged to Cousin Garland during his courtship, though Cousin Garland, after six years of polished deportment, had married a widow who laughed loudly and kept a tobacco shop. Abner took the book down and retired with it to the woodhouse.

There, seated upon an overturned nail keg, he entered civilization.

The book was severe but encouraging. It told him how to bow, how to enter a room, how to leave one, how to accept a cup of tea, how to decline a cup of tea, how to conduct himself at weddings, funerals, boating parties, musicales, and fires. It warned him against discussing politics with ladies, placing his hat upon a piano, coughing into another person’s face, monopolizing conversation, or appearing either too eager or too indifferent.

The section entitled “The Formal Call” shone like a lamp.

“A call,” the book announced, “should ordinarily occupy from fifteen to twenty minutes. The caller, having presented his card, enters with quiet self-possession. He does not perch upon the edge of his chair, nor does he betray embarrassment by twisting his hat. Let a rich stream of conversation flow, avoiding alike the stagnant pools of silence and the noisy cataracts of frivolity.”

Abner read this twice.

The rich stream troubled him. He had conversed with Champe many times, but chiefly in such expressions as “Give me that,” “You’re scared,” “I am not,” and “If you tell, I’ll kill you.” Whether these constituted a stream, and whether its mineral content was socially desirable, he could not decide.

Another paragraph counseled the inexperienced caller to secure, when possible, the companionship of a friend of composure and tact.

Abner shut the book. Ross Dillard was plainly selected by fate.

Ross lived three houses away, behind a picket fence from which every third picket was absent. He was discovered in the stable loft, lying on his stomach and reading a paper about pirates. His red hair stood in a crest where he had pushed it back with dirty fingers, and his freckles advertised a rich soil.

“Ross,” said Abner, “how would you like to go into society?”

Ross held his place in the paper with one thumb.

“What society?”

“Society.”

“What does it do?”

“It don’t do anything. You go into it.”

Ross considered this uncertain pleasure.

“Do they have anything to eat?”

“That isn’t the point. I’m going to make a formal call on Champe Claiborne this afternoon, and I want you to go along.”

Ross rolled over and stared.

“You’re going to what?”

“Call. Pay a call. A gentleman’s call.”

“You owe her something?”

“No, fool. It’s social.”

Ross looked at the long trousers. Enlightenment dawned, though without admiration.

“Oh,” he said. “It’s them.”

Abner mounted the loft ladder another rung.

“The book says a gentleman should take along a friend of composure and tact.”

“What’s tact?”

“Knowing what to say.”

“I don’t know what to say to Champe except she’s got my pocketknife.”

“You won’t have to talk much. I’ll lead the conversation.”

“Then what do you need me for?”

This was a question not adequately treated in the manual.

“For support,” said Abner at last.

“I ain’t goin’.”

Abner opened the book and read aloud the passage concerning the social advantages accruing to the polished young gentleman. He added certain original observations. He pictured the Claiborne parlor glowing with hospitality, iced lemonade passing in tall glasses, cakes upon silver plates, Champe subdued by admiration, and the entire household impressed by their manly bearing. He hinted that girls generally preferred boys who had served their novitiate in polite society. He suggested that Ross’s present refusal arose from fear.

This last argument, though primitive, had survived all changes of fashion.

“I ain’t scared,” Ross said.

“Then come.”

“I don’t want to.”

“Because you’re scared.”

“I’m not.”

“Then come.”

Ross sighed. Oh, youth—youth—youth, with its rash promises extracted in haylofts and redeemed in collars!

“All right,” he said. “But if she laughs, I’m leaving.”

The expedition was fixed for five o’clock. The book recommended late afternoon, but warned against the dinner hour. Neither boy knew the Claiborne dinner hour. Abner maintained that rich people never had regular meals, but ate whenever servants carried food past them.

There remained clothing, conversation, and cards.

Ross possessed no long trousers except a black pair inherited from his brother, who had died of pneumonia at twenty-one and had been five inches taller. Mrs. Dillard, after hearing that Ross was invited to the Claibornes’, turned up the legs, tightened the waistband by violent means, and furnished him with a white collar of such moral rigidity that it seemed designed to prevent not only slouching but sin.

“You mind your manners,” she said. “Don’t you run through their flower beds, and don’t ask for anything.”

“We’re making a call,” Ross explained.

“That’s nice. Be home before dark.”

The ease with which she received this announcement offended him. He had anticipated questions, astonishment, perhaps a maternal tear at his first social enterprise. Instead, she tied his necktie, wiped one of his ears with a damp corner of her apron, and sent him away smelling faintly of soap and resentment.

At Abner’s house the preparations were military. Abner polished his shoes until their cracks shone. He wetted his hair and combed it into dark, parallel ridges. He selected a tie of deep purple, rejected it as too ardent, chose a black one as too funereal, and returned to the purple with the judgment that ardor, properly controlled, was suitable in a caller.

Then came the cards.

A gentleman presented his card. The manual was immovable on this point. Abner had no engraved cards, but civilization could not be permitted to fail for want of a printing press. With stiff white paper, a ruler, and his father’s pen, he manufactured two:

**MR. ABNER TALCOTT**

**MR. ROSS DILLARD**

Ross’s name ran uphill, and the final D in Dillard resembled a fishhook; nevertheless, when the cards lay side by side on the table, they had a cold metropolitan beauty.

“What do we do with ’em?” Ross asked.

“Hand them to the servant.”

“What if there isn’t one?”

“There’s always one at the Claibornes’.”

“What does the servant do?”

“Takes them to the lady.”

“What if Champe’s on the porch and sees us?”

Abner frowned and consulted the manual. The manual, composed for homes with vestibules, footmen, and dependable architecture, had not foreseen Champe sitting on the porch steps shelling peas.

“We ask for her,” he said.

“What if she says, ‘Here I am’?”

“We don’t pay attention. We send in the cards.”

“What if she comes and gets them herself?”

“She won’t.”

“What if she does?”

“Ross, if you keep trying to ruin everything, you can stay home.”

Ross rubbed one polished shoe against his trouser leg.

“I wish I could.”

They rehearsed the call in the parlor. A straight-backed chair represented Champe. Abner entered, bowed, and said, “Good afternoon, Miss Claiborne. I trust I find you well.”

Ross, acting as Champe, replied, “You know I’m well. You saw me at church.”

“That is not what she’ll say. She’ll say, ‘Quite well, thank you. And you?’”

“What do you say then?”

“‘Never better, I assure you.’”

“What if you ain’t?”

“You say it anyway.”

“What if you’ve got the stomachache?”

“A gentleman doesn’t have the stomachache during a call.”

Ross received this evidence of social superiority in silence.

They proceeded to conversation. Weather was safe, provided it did not become technical. Travel was excellent, though neither had traveled farther than the county seat. Books were permissible. Personal compliments must be delicate.

“If she says, ‘That’s a pretty tie,’” Abner instructed, “I say, ‘You flatter me.’”

“What if she says it’s ugly?”

“She won’t.”

“What if she does?”

“Then I say—” Abner searched the book. “I say, ‘You are pleased to be severe.’”

Ross began to grin.

“And if she asks your opinion,” Abner continued, “you must not answer too abruptly. If she says, ‘Which flower do you admire?’ you say, ‘Name yours.’”

“What if I like sunflowers and she likes roses?”

“You say, ‘You flatter us.’”

“That don’t mean anything.”

“It’s etiquette.”

They practiced the rich stream. It flowed badly, spread into marshes, vanished underground, and twice became entangled in Ross’s pocketknife grievance. Yet by half past four Abner felt that enough phrases had been stored to carry them through twenty minutes, if no one introduced a wholly unreasonable subject.

At a quarter to five the two young gentlemen set forth.

The white road to the Claiborne place had never appeared so public. Ordinarily they ran along it, kicked dust, chased grasshoppers, and shouted at passing wagons. Today every gate seemed occupied by an eye. Mrs. Braddock, watering geraniums, called, “My, my! Where are you boys bound, dressed fit to bury somebody?”

Neither answered. They bowed slightly and moved on.

Ross carried his hat in both hands. Abner had ordered this, though they were still outdoors. His collar had already begun to wilt. The cards lay in Abner’s breast pocket, where he touched them every fifteen steps to make sure that society had not escaped.

At the locust grove they stopped.

Beyond the trees stood the Claiborne house, broad, cool, and unconcerned. Four people occupied the front porch. Champe was in the swing. Her mother, whom everybody called Aunt Missouri whether related or not, sat sewing near the door. Mr. Claiborne lay back with a newspaper over his face. Champe’s younger sister, Babe, was arranging pebbles on the steps.

The callers retreated behind a locust tree.

“They’re all out there,” Ross whispered.

“Of course they are. People receive in the parlor.”

“They ain’t in the parlor.”

“We ring, and the servant shows us in.”

“What if Aunt Missouri says hello?”

“We bow.”

“What if Champe says, ‘What are you doing with them clothes on?’”

“We maintain our self-possession.”

Abner consulted the book once more. The sentence “Enter without awkward hesitation” had acquired the aspect of an accusation.

They advanced from the grove.

Champe saw them first. She stopped the swing with one foot and stared. Babe looked up, then ran into the house crying, “Mama, look at Abner’s legs!”

Aunt Missouri lifted her eyes from the sewing.

“Well, bless my soul,” she said. “If it isn’t Ab and Ross. Come on up, boys.”

This was not the expected form.

Abner had prepared for a servant, a card tray, an interval of dignified waiting, and then Champe’s entrance. He had not prepared for Aunt Missouri’s cheerful voice traveling across the yard. She stood between him and formal society like a lion in the way—a kind lion, a hospitable lion, a lion who might offer preserves, but a lion nevertheless.

They reached the porch and removed hats already removed.

“Good evening,” Abner said faintly.

“Good evening,” Ross echoed.

Mr. Claiborne lowered his newspaper.

“Hello, young gentlemen. Running for office?”

Champe made a sound suspiciously like a choke. She had noticed the purple tie.

Abner’s right hand crept toward his breast pocket. This was the psychological moment. He should produce the cards, request that they be presented, and ask if Miss Claiborne was at home. Unfortunately Miss Claiborne was six feet away, staring directly at him. To ask whether she was at home seemed idiotic; to hand her mother a card seemed worse; to hand the card to Champe herself seemed, under Ross’s questioning, to have been outlawed.

His hand came away empty.

“We—we were passing,” he said.

Ross turned upon him a look of injured astonishment. They had walked half a mile specifically not to be passing.

“Well, I’m glad you passed,” Aunt Missouri said. “Sit down.”

There were chairs. There was the porch rail. There were steps. There was the swing beside Champe. Each place contained a separate form of peril.

The boys selected two chairs near the edge of the porch and sat with their hats clutched to their stomachs. They did not lean back. They did not cross their legs. They did not permit any part of themselves to suggest repose. They perched, in direct violation of the manual, like two young saplings weakened at the root.

A pregnant silence followed.

“Hot today,” said Mr. Claiborne.

Abner brightened. Weather!

“Unseasonably so,” he replied.

“Is it?” asked Champe. “It’s July.”

Ross examined his hat.

Aunt Missouri’s needle moved steadily. “How’s your mother, Ab?”

“Quite well, thank you. And you?”

“I’m tolerable.”

“Never better, I assure you,” said Abner.

Aunt Missouri paused. Mr. Claiborne lowered the paper again. Champe’s eyes widened.

Abner felt a scorching realization travel from his collar to his shoes. He had given the response belonging to himself as though it belonged to Aunt Missouri, or perhaps had assured the family that Aunt Missouri was never better without medical authority.

Ross tried to rescue him.

“We’ve been reading books,” he announced.

Abner kicked him.

“What kind?” Champe asked.

“Pirates,” said Ross, abandoning the endangered subject of etiquette.

Babe came out carrying a rag doll. She stood before Abner and inspected the new trousers minutely.

“Are you going to a funeral?”

“No,” he said.

“Why are your pants so big?”

“They are not big.”

“They wrinkle up at the bottom.”

“Run along, Babe,” said Aunt Missouri, smiling into her sewing.

Babe did not run along. She touched the crease at Abner’s knee with one finger.

“Can you climb a tree in them?”

“A gentleman does not climb trees upon a formal—”

He stopped.

“Upon a what?” Champe asked.

“Nothing.”

Ross’s fingers closed violently around his hat brim. The card in his pocket seemed to burn like concealed treason.

The rich stream of conversation now encountered a dam. Abner searched his memory. Travel. Books. Flowers. He looked toward the garden.

“You have many handsome flowers,” he said to Champe.

“We always have.”

“Which do you admire?”

“Those red ones.”

“Name yours,” said Abner.

“I just did.”

“You flatter us.”

There are silences which are empty, and silences crowded with unseen witnesses. This one contained the entire population of the county.

Mr. Claiborne’s newspaper began to shake. Aunt Missouri bent low over her sewing. Champe stared at Abner for one second, two seconds, three; then she sprang from the swing and went into the house with a violent cough.

Ross whispered, “Let’s cut and run.”

“A call is fifteen to twenty minutes,” Abner whispered back.

“We’ve been here a year.”

It had been eleven minutes.

At thirteen minutes a servant named Martha opened the screen door and announced that supper was ready. Aunt Missouri gathered her work.

“Come wash up, boys.”

The callers did not move.

This was an inferential invitation to supper, an event explicitly forbidden. The manual declared: “A caller must not prolong his stay merely because refreshments appear probable.” But refreshments had not appeared probable; they had sounded a dinner bell.

“We—we can’t stay,” Abner said.

“Nonsense,” Aunt Missouri replied. “Your mothers won’t expect you before dark.”

Ross looked at Abner. Abner looked at Ross. Neither had the strength to explain that their mothers expected them before dark precisely because no one had imagined a formal call would swallow supper.

Mr. Claiborne folded his newspaper. “Come along, statesmen.”

They followed.

In the washroom, Ross seized Abner by the sleeve.

“Give her the card now.”

“To whom?”

“Anybody. Slip it under a plate.”

“That would be vulgar.”

“Then tell Champe.”

“Not at supper.”

“We’ll be here forever.”

“After supper we rise and thunder out our farewells.”

They did not rise. They did not thunder out anything.

Supper extended before them in courses not because the Claibornes practiced European dining, but because Martha repeatedly remembered something left in the kitchen. There were fried chicken, biscuits, corn, tomatoes, beans, preserves, and a peach cobbler whose arrival destroyed Ross’s remaining loyalty to the fifteen-minute rule.

Etiquette made every mouthful dangerous. Abner declined butter, then recalled that abrupt refusal was discourteous and accepted it. He tried to converse without food in his mouth, which left him no time to eat; then, fearing that his abstinence might seem critical of the table, he ate too rapidly and choked on corn.

Champe sat opposite him.

“Do gentlemen always turn purple when they swallow?” she asked.

“You are pleased to be severe,” he gasped.

Mr. Claiborne coughed into his napkin.

Ross, whose collar prevented him from looking down without bending from the waist, lost a bean. It rolled across the tablecloth and stopped beside Aunt Missouri’s plate. Babe pursued its course with loud commentary.

“Ross threw a bean at Mama.”

“I did not.”

“I saw it roll.”

“It fell.”

“Beans don’t fall sideways.”

“Babe,” Aunt Missouri said, “eat your supper and quit prosecuting the company.”

Company! The word encouraged Abner. They were recognized as callers. Perhaps no declaration was needed. Perhaps the cards could be left discreetly upon departure, fulfilling the spirit of social law.

Under cover of the cobbler he removed the cards and held them on his knee.

Ross saw them.

“Now,” he mouthed.

Abner shook his head.

“Now.”

“To who?”

Ross indicated Champe with his eyebrows so violently that Babe noticed.

“What’s wrong with your face?” she asked.

“Nothing.”

“You keep twitching at Champe.”

Ross dropped his spoon.

Champe leaned across the table. “Is there something you want to tell me?”

The moment arrived, splendid and terrible. Abner could have placed the card beside her plate. He could have said, “We have called.” He could have risen, bowed, and brought the enterprise to a victorious conclusion.

Instead he put both cards in his mouth.

It was not intentional. Aunt Missouri turned toward him just as his hand rose; panic completed the gesture. For one dreadful instant he sat with the corner of his own social identity protruding between his lips. Then he coughed, covered his mouth, and transferred the damp cards into his pocket.

“What are you eating?” asked Babe.

“Nothing.”

“I saw paper.”

“You did not.”

“Was it a note?”

“No!”

Champe’s smile grew thoughtful.

After supper the family repaired to the parlor. The boys believed departure possible, but hope, like a young chicken, is most vulnerable just outside the coop. Before Abner could announce anything, Mr. Claiborne set out a checkerboard and challenged Ross.

Ross dared not refuse. A gentleman, said the manual, should adapt himself gracefully to innocent amusement. He adapted for forty-five minutes while Abner sat beside Champe on the sofa, separated from her by his hat.

“Why are you holding that?” she asked.

“A gentleman should never place his hat on the piano.”

“You’re not near the piano.”

“No.”

“You could put it on the floor.”

“It might get stepped on.”

“Put it on the table.”

“That would be improper.”

“Then wear it.”

Abner suspected mockery, but could not prove it.

Aunt Missouri asked Champe to play. Champe went to the piano and performed “The Blue Bells of Scotland” with energetic inaccuracies. The manual advised the young gentleman, following music, to express restrained appreciation.

“You flatter us,” Abner said when she finished.

This time there could be no mistake. Mr. Claiborne got up and went out on the porch. Through the open window came a series of explosive coughs.

Ross, defeated at checkers because his attention had been fixed upon escape, joined Abner near the door.

“Let’s go,” he whispered.

“Wait till there’s a break.”

There was never a break. Babe recited a poem. Aunt Missouri told a story about a minister and a mule. Mr. Claiborne returned and proposed that Ross show Champe the card trick he had performed at the church social. Ross denied knowledge of all cards, natural or supernatural. Lemonade appeared, followed by cake, proving that Abner’s original prophecy had been accurate but tragically late.

Darkness pressed against the windows.

“Your mothers will be wondering,” Aunt Missouri said at last.

The boys rose so suddenly that their knees struck the table.

“Yes, ma’am,” they said together.

Aunt Missouri glanced toward the road. “It’s fixing to storm. Missouri clouds, too. You boys had better wait till it passes.”

A low roll of thunder confirmed her hospitality.

“We can make it,” Ross said.

Lightning whitened the room. Rain struck the porch roof with the instantaneous violence of thrown gravel.

“No, you can’t,” Mr. Claiborne said. “Sit down.”

They sat.

The storm settled over the house with professional thoroughness. Water poured from the eaves. The road vanished. The clock struck nine, then ten. Abner’s collar had ceased to be a collar and become a damp recollection. Ross’s turned-up trousers sagged around his ankles. Their hats, crushed by hours of moral pressure, no longer possessed form.

At ten-thirty Aunt Missouri said the sentence that broke them.

“Martha, make up the spare room for these boys.”

Abner stared.

Ross stared.

Babe clapped.

“They’re going to sleep here!”

“No,” said Abner.

Everyone looked at him.

He had only to speak. He had only to say, “Madam, we came to pay a formal call upon your daughter, and having exceeded the prescribed twenty minutes by approximately five hours, we must withdraw regardless of atmospheric conditions.” It was a long sentence, but desperation might have carried it.

Instead he said, “I mean—Mama doesn’t know.”

“I’ll send word if the rain lets up,” Aunt Missouri replied. “She’ll know you’re safe.”

“We could sleep in the barn,” Ross suggested wildly.

“The spare room’s got two beds.”

“We’re used to barns.”

“Ross,” said Mr. Claiborne, “you’re not a horse.”

The family laughed, not cruelly, but with the terrible ease of persons who are at home. The boys were conducted upstairs.

The spare room contained two narrow beds beneath a framed text reading, *Be Ye Also Ready*. Champe placed a lamp on the table and wished them good night with exaggerated courtesy.

“I trust I find you well,” she said.

Abner whitened.

“Never better, I assure you,” Ross replied, and shut the door in her face.

They listened to her laughter retreat down the hall.

Then Ross turned.

“We’ve got to get out.”

“It’s raining.”

“Through the window.”

“We’re on the second floor.”

“Down the vine.”

“That’s ivy. It won’t hold.”

“Then tie the sheets together.”

“That’s stealing.”

“We won’t take ’em with us!”

Abner sat on one bed, his long trousers ballooning around him.

“We’ll leave at daylight.”

“We never gave her the cards.”

Abner brought them out. They had merged into one soft, purple-edged mass from the lemonade spilled at supper.

Ross contemplated the ruin.

“All this,” he said, “and we ain’t called yet.”

“We have called.”

“We said we were passing.”

“We sat in the parlor.”

“We ate supper.”

“Callers sometimes—”

“Callers don’t get put to bed.”

That was unanswerable.

They undressed to their shirts and drawers, placing the ceremonial clothes over chair backs. Without long trousers Abner’s manhood suffered a rapid contraction. He became again a boy with thin shins and bruised knees, lying awake in a strange room while rain whispered in the gutters.

From below came muffled voices, then laughter.

“They know,” Ross said.

“They do not.”

“Champe knows.”

“She suspects.”

“They’re laughing at us.”

“They’re probably laughing at Mr. Claiborne’s story.”

The laughter rose again, and in it could plainly be distinguished Champe’s piercing note.

Abner pulled the sheet over his head.

Morning arrived offensively clear.

Sunlight entered the spare room as if no social catastrophe had occurred. A rooster crowed in the yard. Somewhere below, dishes clattered and bacon hissed. The boys dressed in silence. Their collars were beyond restoration. Abner’s purple tie had acquired a list to port. Ross’s trousers, having lost one pin in the night, were longer on the left side.

“Soon as we get downstairs,” Ross said, “we tell her.”

“Before breakfast?”

“Before anything.”

“Perhaps we should wait until we’re received.”

“We’ve been received till I’m sick of it.”

They descended.

The entire household sat in the dining room: Aunt Missouri, Mr. Claiborne, Champe, Babe, Grandmother Claiborne, two visiting cousins who had not been present the evening before, Martha at the sideboard, and the gardener visible through the open window. The audience had increased by unexplained but malign natural processes.

Every face turned.

“Well!” Aunt Missouri cried. “Here come our callers.”

The word struck both boys like a broom handle.

Champe bent over her plate. Her shoulders shook.

Mr. Claiborne stood with solemn ceremony. “Good morning, Mr. Talcott. Good morning, Mr. Dillard. I trust you rested after the fatigues of your visit.”

“You flatter us,” Champe murmured.

The room collapsed into laughter.

Babe trembled like chocolate pudding. Grandmother Claiborne wiped her eyes. Even Martha turned toward the sideboard, though her back betrayed her. The boys remained in the doorway, hats in hand, their faces passing successively through red, scarlet, and a shade for which nature has provided no flower.

They knew. Everybody knew.

During the night, their mystery had been examined, compared with evidence, and solved. Perhaps Champe had seen the cards. Perhaps Aunt Missouri had heard Abner’s unfinished “formal.” Perhaps no evidence was necessary beyond two collars, two hats, and six hours of unexplained agony.

Aunt Missouri recovered first.

“Come eat, boys. Formal callers need breakfast.”

“We were just leaving,” Abner said.

“Not before you tell Champe what you came for,” said Mr. Claiborne.

A path opened before them. It led to Champe, who sat with her chin in her hands and malice sparkling in her eyes.

Abner glanced at Ross. Ross glanced at Abner.

“Fire away,” Ross whispered.

“You do it.”

“It was your call.”

“You came too.”

“As support.”

“Then support.”

Aunt Missouri poured coffee with maddening patience.

“Well?”

Abner’s hand entered his pocket and drew forth the pulpy remains of the cards. He attempted to separate them. Ross Dillard’s final D tore away and adhered to Abner Talcott’s name.

“We—we—” Abner began.

All conversation ceased. Even the bacon seemed to stop sizzling.

“We came—”

A horse galloped into the yard.

Never did rescue approach with a more heroic sound. Never was rescue more deceptively mounted.

A boy from the Talcott place leaped from a mule at the back gate and ran to the porch. It was Abner’s younger brother, Sam, barefoot, breathless, and delighted with his commission.

“Ab!” he shouted through the screen. “Ma says you’re to come home this minute!”

Abner’s relief lasted one second.

Sam opened the door and delivered the remainder.

“She says if you’re not home before I get back, she’s coming after you with the buggy whip. She says you took Pa’s good pen, left the woodhouse lamp burning, and went off without filling the kindling box. She says long pants don’t make a man out of a natural-born fool.”

Silence followed—not a pregnant silence, nor an expectant silence, nor any silence known to manuals of deportment. It was the vast, crystalline stillness which precedes universal destruction.

Then Babe squealed.

Champe threw back her head and laughed.

The household followed. Mr. Claiborne struck the table. Aunt Missouri protested, “Now, now,” while laughing helplessly herself. Grandmother Claiborne removed her spectacles because tears had rendered them useless. Sam, realizing he had accomplished something great, grinned at everybody.

Abner looked neither right nor left. His face emptied of expression. He placed the ruined cards on the nearest table, jammed his crushed hat upon his head, and walked toward the door with the mechanical dignity of a condemned prince.

At the threshold his nerve broke.

He ran.

Across the porch he flew, down the steps, over the gravel, through Aunt Missouri’s bed of white petunias, and into the road. His long trousers flapped at his ankles; his purple tie streamed over one shoulder; his mother’s messenger sprang onto the mule and galloped after him, shouting further details of the domestic indictment.

Ross started too.

Loyalty, habit, and terror propelled him as far as the porch steps. He had endured the road, the collars, the rich stream, the bean, the card, the checkerboard, the storm, the spare room, breakfast, and the buggy whip by association. Nothing remained but flight.

Then Champe laughed behind him.

It was not the household’s laughter now. It was hers alone—bright, victorious, intolerable.

Ross stopped.

There are moments when a boy’s whole character, previously scattered among fears, boasts, bruises, stolen apples, and unfinished lessons, gathers itself without warning into one compact and dangerous purpose. No book announces such a moment. No rule prepares for it. Etiquette, standing at a safe distance, disapproves.

Ross turned.

Champe stood just inside the dining-room doorway, one hand against the frame. Her red hair caught the morning sun. She expected him to say something foolish, or angry, or borrowed. She expected another “You flatter us,” perhaps. The whole family expected it.

Ross climbed the steps.

His knees were weak. His left trouser leg dragged. His collar leaned outward like a broken gate. Yet he advanced.

“What did you come for, Mr. Dillard?” Champe asked.

Ross looked at her. Behind her were Aunt Missouri, Mr. Claiborne, Babe, Grandmother, the cousins, Martha, Sam’s abandoned dust, breakfast, society, and judgment. The world was full of eyes.

He threw his hat on the floor.

Before Champe could move, he caught her by both shoulders and kissed her squarely upon the mouth.

It was not a polished kiss. It was not restrained, graceful, or delicate. It had no resemblance to anything in *The Young Gentleman’s Social Guide and Manual of Polite Deportment*. It was brief, loud, desperate, and astonishingly successful.

Ross released her.

“There,” he said. “That’s what I came for.”

Nobody laughed.

Champe stood motionless, her freckles nearly hidden by color. Babe’s mouth formed a perfect circle. Aunt Missouri held the coffee pot suspended in midair. Mr. Claiborne stared at Ross with an expression in which outrage struggled unsuccessfully against admiration.

Ross picked up his hat, bowed—not well, but independently—and walked down the steps.

He had reached the gate when the first pebble struck the fence beside him.

He looked back.

Champe was on the porch, scarlet-faced, gathering ammunition from Babe’s carefully arranged collection.

“You come back here, Ross Dillard!”

Another stone flew. Ross ducked, laughing.

“You stop, or I’ll kill you!”

A third pebble clipped his hat. He placed it firmly on his head and ran down the white road, not in panic now, but in triumph, while Champe pursued him to the gate and threw until the last of Babe’s pebbles was gone.

Far ahead, Abner’s purple tie vanished around the bend, hastened by the remembered buggy whip and the neglected kindling. Ross followed at leisure. His collar was ruined, his trousers ridiculous, his card dissolved, and his reputation, by every civilized standard, irrecoverable.

But he had made his call.

The town of Bellweather had no clocks.

There were old clock towers, certainly. One rose above the courthouse, another above the abandoned railway station, and a third—small, green-roofed, and forever occupied by pigeons—stood at the end of Market Street. But their hands had been removed generations ago, leaving only pale circles open to the weather.

In Bellweather, time was kept by the bells.

At dawn, the east tower rang once. At midday, the courthouse rang six measured notes. At sunset, all three towers answered one another across the slate rooftops, their overlapping voices sending merchants to their ledgers, children to their suppers, and fishermen home from the river.

No one asked how many minutes had passed. No one complained of being late. A thing began when its bell rang and ended when the next bell sounded.

Only Mara Vale kept a clock.

It had belonged to her father, who had disappeared when she was nine. The clock was small enough to fit in her palm, with a brass case scratched by years of travel. Inside, two black hands moved beneath cracked glass. It ticked quietly, stubbornly, dividing each day into invisible pieces.

Her father had called it a pocket watch.

“You must never show it to anyone,” he had told her.

“Why?”

“Because people fear what measures them.”

At nine, Mara had not understood. At twenty-three, she understood enough to keep it hidden under the loose floorboard beneath her bed.

She brought it out at night.

Tick.

Tick.

Tick.

The sound was so delicate that it seemed impossible it could contain the whole world. Yet by watching the hands, Mara could predict the bells. She knew the dawn bell rang at six, the courthouse at twelve, and the sunset bells at six in winter and nine in summer. The bell keepers pretended to read the sky, but Mara knew they must possess hidden clocks of their own.

She also knew the west tower had been ringing incorrectly.

At first, the difference was small. Its sunset bell came perhaps one minute before the others. Then two minutes. By the first snow, it rang nearly a quarter of an hour early.

Bellweather began to change.

Shopkeepers shut their doors while customers were still inside. Bakers took loaves from ovens before the crust had browned. Children arrived home breathless, scolded by parents who could not explain how supper had come so soon. The courthouse bell remained true, but uncertainty spread. People began waiting for the west tower, suspecting it knew something the others did not.

“The days are shortening,” the mayor announced.

“It is winter,” said the schoolmistress.

“Not like this,” he replied.

Soon the west bell crept into the afternoon.

No one challenged it. Bells defined the hours; therefore, if the bell rang, sunset had arrived. Curtains were drawn against bright skies. Lamps were lit. Workers hurried home while sunlight still flashed on the river.

The town lost nearly an hour each day.

Only Mara knew how much.

She worked in the municipal archive, a narrow stone building that smelled of dust, wet wool, and binding glue. Most of her duties involved copying birth records and sorting property claims. Bellweather recorded many things—names, debts, marriages, floods—but never hours or minutes.

One cold morning, while shelving documents from the courthouse cellar, Mara found a sealed box marked:

TEMPORAL IRREGULARITIES  
BY ORDER OF THE FIRST COUNCIL  
DO NOT OPEN BETWEEN BELLS

The warning was absurd. Everything in Bellweather happened between bells.

Mara waited until the archivist went to lunch, then broke the seal.

Inside lay a stack of letters, a map of the town, and a thin book bound in faded blue leather. On its cover, someone had stamped a title:

A HISTORY OF THE FOURTH BELL

Mara read standing beside the shelf.

According to the book, Bellweather had once possessed a fourth tower on the hill north of town. Its bell did not announce dawn, noon, or sunset. It rang at midnight, when no honest citizen was expected to hear it.

The fourth bell had a single purpose: it returned to the town whatever time had been lost during the day.

A minute wasted in an argument, an hour spent waiting for bad news, an afternoon forgotten in grief—all were gathered by the midnight bell and released into dreams. People woke restored, carrying no memory of the extra time, only the sense that life was spacious and the future far away.

Then, during a winter of famine, the mayor ordered the fourth bell rung before midnight. He wanted a longer day in which to arrange supplies.

The stolen hours returned all at once.

Fruit ripened and rotted on branches. Babies became children between one breath and the next. Paint peeled from doors. The river froze, thawed, and flooded Market Street before anyone could run.

The council tore down the northern tower. Its stones were scattered, and its bell was buried where no map would show.

Mara turned to the map in the box.

A red circle marked the northern hill.

Beneath it, in handwriting she recognized immediately, were four words:

The bell is still hungry.

Her father’s handwriting.

Mara sat heavily on the floor.

All her life, people had offered explanations for Elias Vale’s disappearance. He had drowned in the river. He had fled his debts. He had joined a traveling theater. Her mother, before she died, had said only, “Your father found a question he could not leave unanswered.”

Now Mara held the question in her hands.

She took the letters home and read them by candlelight. They had been written by bell keepers, mayors, and archivists over two centuries. Most described minor irregularities: bells ringing without being touched, shadows pointing east at noon, citizens remembering events that had not happened.

The final letter was from her father.

Mara,

If you are reading this, I failed to return.

The fourth bell was not destroyed. It was buried, but a bell cannot be silenced merely by surrounding it with earth. It has continued to collect lost time. Every delayed farewell, every sleepless night, every year wished away—it has kept them all.

Now the ground above it is beginning to ring.

If the bell wakes, the town will receive centuries at once.

I have gone to quiet it.

Do not follow me.

With love,  
Father

Mara read the letter twice. Then she lifted the floorboard and took out the watch.

Its hands had stopped.

The silence frightened her more than any bell.

Outside, the west tower rang sunset, though the sky was still white with morning.

Doors slammed throughout Bellweather. People cried out in confusion. A horse bolted down Market Street, dragging an empty cart. The courthouse bell answered with six notes, then the station bell began, and soon all three towers were ringing wildly.

Mara put on her coat and ran north.

Beyond the last houses, the road narrowed to a frozen path. Snow covered the hill, except at its summit, where a circle of black earth steamed in the cold.

The ground hummed beneath her boots.

She found the buried tower’s entrance behind a curtain of dead ivy: a stone arch descending into darkness. The stairs below were narrow and slick. Mara lit a candle, though the flame bent sideways as if blown by a wind she could not feel.

At the bottom waited a door of green copper.

There was no handle, only a shallow circular hollow.

Mara placed the pocket watch inside it.

The door opened.

Beyond lay an enormous chamber. Roots twisted through its ceiling. In the center hung the fourth bell, black with age and taller than a house. Though buried beneath the hill, it was suspended from a wooden frame untouched by rot.

A man stood beside it.

He wore a gray coat. One hand rested against the bronze. His hair was dark, and his face was exactly as Mara remembered it.

“Father?”

He turned.

For him, she realized, no time had passed.

“Mara?” His face went pale. “What are you doing here?”

She crossed the chamber before he could move and threw her arms around him. He felt real—warm, solid, trembling.

“You’ve been gone fourteen years,” she said.

He pulled back and stared at her. “No. I came down this morning.”

“The bell took your time.”

Elias looked toward the great dark curve beside them.

A low vibration traveled through the chamber. Dust rose from the floor. Somewhere overhead, all the bells of Bellweather rang together.

“We have to leave,” Mara said.

“We can’t.” He pointed to a rope descending from the bell’s interior. “I stopped the clapper, but only by holding it outside the current. If I release it, the bell will ring.”

Mara saw then that his left hand was not merely resting against the bronze. It disappeared into the bell’s shadow, blurred as though submerged in deep water.

“How long can you hold it?”

“For me? Perhaps another hour.”

“For the town?”

He looked at her grown face and understood.

“Oh,” he whispered.

The chamber shuddered. A crack opened in the floor. Within it, Mara glimpsed impossible things: summer grass, autumn leaves, snow melting and freezing in a single heartbeat.

Elias reached for her with his free hand.

“You must go.”

“I didn’t come to lose you again.”

“If the bell rings, Bellweather will age hundreds of years.”

“Then we stop it.”

“I have tried.”

“You tried alone.”

Mara took the pocket watch from the copper door. It remained still, its hands fixed at six minutes past eleven.

“What made this stop?” she asked.

“The bell. Clocks measure time, but this place is filled with too much of it. Like lowering a cup into the sea.”

“Can the watch hold any?”

“A second or two, perhaps.”

“Then we give the bell somewhere else to ring.”

Elias shook his head. “A bell of this size—”

“Doesn’t need a large place. Only a large amount of time.”

She opened the watch and tore off its minute hand.

Her father stared at her. “What are you doing?”

“Making room.”

The watch ticked once.

The sound echoed through the chamber like a stone dropped into a well.

The bell answered.

A deep note trembled inside the bronze, though the clapper had not moved. Mara’s candle went out. Images poured around them: houses rising from bare earth, generations crossing Market Street, faces appearing and vanishing like sparks. She saw her mother as a child. She saw the river change course. She saw her father holding her on the day she was born.

Then she saw the future.

Bellweather abandoned. Vines covering the courthouse. The clockless towers collapsing one by one.

All of it rushed toward the broken watch.

Its brass case grew hot in Mara’s hand.

“The bell is emptying,” Elias shouted above the roar. “Close the watch!”

“How?”

“The hand! Put it back!”

Mara tried, but the minute hand slipped from her fingers. It struck the floor and vanished into a crack.

The watch pulled harder.

Years streamed past. The wooden frame above the bell whitened, splintered, and became whole again. Roots shrank into seeds. Elias’s face flickered between youth and old age.

If the watch continued drawing time, Mara understood, it would not stop with the bell. It would swallow the chamber, the hill, perhaps the town itself.

She looked at the frozen hour on its face.

Six minutes past eleven.

The watch did not need its old hand. It needed an ending.

Mara seized the hour hand and turned it forward.

The mechanism fought her. She forced it past midnight.

The case snapped shut.

Silence fell.

The great bell split from crown to rim.

For several moments, neither Mara nor Elias moved. Then his trapped hand slipped free. He stumbled backward, and she caught him.

Above them, the wooden frame groaned.

They ran.

The stairs twisted beneath their feet. Stones fell from the ceiling. Elias pushed Mara through the copper doorway just as the chamber collapsed behind them.

They emerged onto the hill at dusk.

True dusk.

Bellweather lay below, its windows glowing gold. The three towers stood silent against a violet sky.

Mara’s watch was gone. In her palm remained only a circle of tarnished brass, smooth and empty.

Her father looked down at the town.

“Fourteen years,” he said.

“Yes.”

“Your mother?”

Mara did not answer.

He closed his eyes. The grief that crossed his face seemed to age him more surely than any bell could have done.

They walked home together.

In the days that followed, Bellweather struggled to decide what time it was. The west tower never rang again. Its bell had cracked at the same moment as the one beneath the hill. The courthouse keeper confessed that his hidden clock had stopped months earlier. The station keeper admitted he had been listening to the courthouse. The keeper of the east tower simply vanished, leaving behind three empty bottles and a note that read, I was always guessing.

For the first time in its history, the town had no reliable bells.

Confusion became argument. Argument became panic. Merchants opened before dawn. Teachers dismissed lessons after ten minutes or kept children until their parents came searching. The mayor formed a Committee for the Restoration of Proper Sequence, which met for so long that everyone forgot when it had begun.

Mara watched the disorder for a week.

Then she climbed the courthouse tower.

The old mechanism filled an upper room with gears, cables, and rust. At its center stood a narrow iron shaft where a clock had once been connected to the bell.

Elias joined her, carrying a wooden box.

Inside was a new clock.

He had built it from scraps in his workshop: brass gears, a silver spring, and two black hands beneath clear glass. It was larger than the pocket watch and far less elegant, but it ticked steadily.

“Will they fear it?” Mara asked.

“Probably.”

“Will they break it?”

“Possibly.”

“Then why build it?”

Her father smiled. “Because people fear what measures them. But sometimes they need to see that measurement is not the same as command.”

They installed the clock behind the tower’s blank white face.

At noon, the courthouse bell rang six notes.

The people of Bellweather gathered in the square. Above them, for the first time in generations, two black hands pointed straight upward.

No one moved.

Then the baker laughed.

It was an uncertain laugh, but others joined him. Shopkeepers reopened their doors. Children who had been hiding from school were discovered and returned to their lessons. The mayor declared that he had supported clocks all along.

Over the following months, Bellweather learned minutes.

Some hated them. Some became obsessed, counting every task and scolding every delay. Others found minutes useful for boiling eggs, meeting friends, and knowing how long to wait before deciding someone was not coming.

Mara kept the town’s official clock. She wound it each morning and corrected it each evening. Yet she refused to let the bells rule every part of the day. Dawn still rang when light touched the eastern roofs. Sunset rang only when the sun disappeared. Weddings began when the couple was ready. Funerals ended when the last story had been told.

Years later, when Elias had grown old in the ordinary way, Mara asked him what had happened to all the time trapped in the fourth bell.

He considered the question.

“Perhaps the watch destroyed it.”

“Time can’t be destroyed.”

“No,” he agreed. “Perhaps it was returned.”

“To whom?”

“To everyone.”

Mara thought of the changes she had noticed since the night beneath the hill. People lingered more often in doorways. Children complained that summer afternoons lasted forever. Grieving families sometimes dreamed of the dead and woke feeling they had spoken for hours.

Her own life seemed neither long nor short. It was simply hers.

On the evening Elias died, the sunset bells rang across Bellweather. Mara sat beside his bed, holding his hand. The final note faded, but she did not rise. The new courthouse clock ticked on the wall.

“I’m sorry,” he murmured. “For losing all those years.”

“You didn’t lose them,” she said.

“No?”

“You left them with me.”

Outside, darkness settled over the town. Lamps appeared one by one, warm against the blue. The clock continued measuring, patient and indifferent.

Mara reached up and stopped its pendulum.

For one night, Bellweather had no hours.

And no one was late.
